highlights: Europe still depends on Algerian gas

frictionVectors.title: European gas leverage
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains state control over major gas assets, but European demand, pricing, and infrastructure access continue to shape export strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability along southern borders increases surveillance and defense costs while exposing Algeria to competing external security initiatives.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese financing exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese lenders and contractors retain a major role in infrastructure, while repayment pressures can constrain Luanda's policy flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore production decline
frictionVectors.details: Maturing oil fields and dependence on foreign operators weaken domestic control over future production and public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's trade infrastructure is strategically vital, but financing, logistics, and regional commerce remain exposed to foreign operators and neighboring-country politics.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel militant pressure
frictionVectors.details: Attacks and recruitment risks in northern Benin are drawing greater external security assistance while challenging state control of border regions.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation pressure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has strengthened its share of diamond value, but continued dependence on De Beers expertise, marketing, and global distribution remains a sovereignty constraint.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals could diversify the economy, but weak downstream processing may leave value capture abroad.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-contract confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater state participation and revenue from gold mining, creating friction with foreign operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: Closer ties with Russian security actors reduce reliance on Western partners but raise concerns over accountability, sanctions exposure, and opaque resource-for-security arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater state control over nickel, rare-earth, and gold projects, but limited capital and technical capacity leave it dependent on foreign operators and trading networks.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Persistent tensions with Rwanda and instability in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo complicate border security, trade access, and Burundi's ability to set an independent regional agenda.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime competition
frictionVectors.details: Mindelo and Praia attract interest from European, North American, and Chinese-linked logistics actors, creating competition over port modernization and maritime-security access.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cape Verde retains strong institutional control, but its small economy remains exposed to externally financed transport, energy, and digital projects and to tourism volatility.

highlights: Oil and timber value captured unevenly

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain important in roads, hydropower, and construction, while financing and project-execution terms can reduce transparency and constrain future fiscal room.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and northern insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside Boko Haram-related insecurity in the Far North, diverts state capacity and threatens transport corridors and extractive projects.

frictionVectors.title: Russian-linked resource access
frictionVectors.details: The government's security relationship with Russian-linked forces has strengthened regime survival but is associated with opaque arrangements around gold, diamonds, and other extractive assets.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and border fragility
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on routes through Cameroon and instability near Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo leave trade, fuel supply, and mining logistics vulnerable to armed groups and external shocks.

highlights: Oil remains the fiscal sovereignty anchor
Sahel and Sudan pressures widen exposure

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-access bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Chad is renegotiating its external security relationships as French influence recedes, while Gulf, Russian, and Western actors compete for access and strategic alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and border-corridor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: State revenues remain heavily tied to oil, while conflict in Sudan and insecurity around Lake Chad threaten transport routes, displacement management, and the government's negotiating position with foreign partners.

highlights: Port and fisheries partnerships diversify slowly

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and French leverage
frictionVectors.details: France retains decisive influence through Mayotte, migration controls, security ties, and development assistance. Moroni continues diplomatic pressure but lacks the economic and military leverage to alter the status quo.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and French actors compete for influence over ports, connectivity, and fisheries. Limited state capacity increases the risk that infrastructure deals deliver weak local returns.

highlights: Critical minerals attract competing foreign blocs

frictionVectors.title: M23, Rwanda, and eastern mineral corridors
frictionVectors.details: The conflict around North and South Kivu continues to weaken Kinshasa's control and expose links between armed groups, regional security interests, and mineral flows. Diplomatic pressure has not yet produced a durable security settlement.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: China remains deeply embedded in copper and cobalt supply chains while the United States, European partners, and Gulf investors seek alternative access and logistics routes. Contract renegotiation and weak oversight limit the state's ability to capture full resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenue remains the backbone of public finance, leaving Brazzaville vulnerable to price swings and opaque contracting. Debt-linked obligations and energy-sector partnerships continue to narrow fiscal and strategic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic and regional infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain a major role in roads, public works, and infrastructure finance, while regional transport projects compete for influence around Pointe-Noire. Weak diversification means external partners can shape economic priorities disproportionately.

highlights: Cocoa and critical minerals test local value capture

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire remains a leading cocoa producer but captures a limited share of downstream value amid volatile prices, climate stress, and buyer concentration. State efforts to improve farmer income and processing capacity face strong external market pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Security spillover and strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability in the Sahel continue to pressure northern border regions and defense planning. France, the United States, China, Turkey, and Gulf actors are competing for commercial and security access as Abidjan seeks greater autonomy.

highlights: Port state balances rival military powers

frictionVectors.title: Foreign bases and sovereignty trade-offs
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its strategic location through hosting American, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities. The arrangement provides revenue and deterrence but makes the country vulnerable to great-power rivalry and limits independent security choices.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and port dependency
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed infrastructure and port-linked obligations remain central to the economy, while Ethiopia's trade access provides Djibouti with vital but asymmetric leverage. Debt servicing, underutilized capacity, and regional competition constrain the gains from its logistics model.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and Gulf-linked asset sales
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal pressure is driving privatization and foreign investment in strategic sectors, creating tension between hard-currency needs and long-term Egyptian control.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, while Egypt views upstream dam operations as a direct threat to agricultural and national security.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature fields and limited diversification leave the state dependent on foreign operators, offshore technology, and volatile energy revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-built strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external contractors remain important to ports, roads, and public works, increasing financing exposure despite formal state ownership.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping routes attract competing regional and external security interests, raising sovereignty risks around access and basing.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining revenues and technical capacity remain tied to external firms, while opaque state structures limit transparency over ownership and resource benefits.

frictionVectors.title: South African economic gravity
frictionVectors.details: Trade, logistics, finance, and energy links with South Africa constrain Eswatini's room for independent economic policy and infrastructure planning.

frictionVectors.title: Land and agricultural control
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, forestry, and commercial land remain concentrated among politically connected and external interests, limiting broad domestic control of productive assets.

frictionVectors.title: Nile diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia has strengthened control over its electricity strategy through the GERD, but unresolved tensions with Egypt and Sudan continue to threaten regional stability.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and telecom access
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on foreign investment in telecommunications and infrastructure bring capital while imposing constraints on policy autonomy and strategic data control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic mining
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for more domestic processing and state leverage over manganese and other minerals, but Chinese, French and other foreign operators remain central to extraction and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors, especially rail links to mineral terminals, remain vulnerable to financing and operational dependence on external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign pressure on fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing by industrial fleets weakens coastal resource sovereignty and exposes enforcement gaps involving foreign vessels.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on external financing and contractors for port, transport and energy upgrades, limiting its autonomy over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and foreign-linked networks
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated gold mining, including operations involving foreign financiers and equipment suppliers, is damaging water systems and challenging state control over extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and energy-sector leverage
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal constraints and dependence on external creditors and power-sector investors narrow policy space over oil, gas and electricity infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou concession power
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-led consortia control major financing, construction and export logistics for Simandou, creating a sovereignty tension despite government efforts to secure infrastructure and local-content gains.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite exports rely on foreign mining firms, rail systems and port facilities, while environmental costs and limited domestic processing constrain Guinea's bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign buyers and trading networks dominate the cashew value chain, leaving producers and the state vulnerable to price shocks and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Cocaine-trafficking corridors
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime, customs and judicial capacity allows transnational trafficking networks to exploit ports and political institutions, undermining effective sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is seeking to rebalance financing away from opaque bilateral borrowing while remaining dependent on external creditors and major transport projects. Port, rail, and energy assets remain sensitive points in negotiations with foreign lenders and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals and energy investment
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital is expanding in geothermal power, renewables, and mineral exploration. Nairobi is strengthening local-content and revenue rules, but enforcement capacity remains uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but leave the kingdom dependent on South African infrastructure, purchasing arrangements, and project financing. Delays and cost overruns continue to constrain national bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-owned manufacturing base
frictionVectors.details: The textile and apparel sector remains heavily reliant on foreign investors and preferential market access. Employment is vulnerable to shifts in United States trade policy, Asian sourcing decisions, and regional competition.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore and gold projects are central to growth but leave Liberia exposed to concession terms, commodity cycles, and foreign operators. The government is under pressure to improve revenue collection, local processing, and community benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, road, and mining-corridor investments are reshaping Liberia's trade geography. Weak institutional capacity increases the risk that infrastructure agreements transfer excessive control over strategic logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil institutions
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest control over production, export terminals, and budget flows. International oil companies and foreign states retain substantial leverage because Libya lacks a unified security and fiscal framework.

frictionVectors.title: Mercenary and military infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign military support, advisers, and security-linked infrastructure remain embedded in Libya's political economy. Their presence constrains sovereign decision-making and raises the risk that energy corridors become bargaining tools in wider regional rivalries.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic minerals and foreign operators
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, ilmenite, and other mineral projects attract major foreign capital while Madagascar struggles to capture greater value through processing and taxation. Environmental disputes and opaque licensing remain recurrent sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, connectivity, and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed ports, telecommunications, and transport projects are increasingly important to Madagascar's integration into Indian Ocean trade. Fiscal weakness limits the government's ability to negotiate equal terms or maintain infrastructure independently.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Policy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on IMF and donor financing constrain policy autonomy. Foreign-exchange shortages continue to limit state capacity and imports of fuel, fertilizer, and machinery.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, graphite, and rare-earth prospects attract foreign investors, but weak transport and power networks leave Malawi with limited bargaining leverage and domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is demanding greater state participation and revenue from industrial gold mining, creating friction with foreign operators while artisanal mining and smuggling remain difficult to control.

frictionVectors.title: Security Dependence and Regional Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian security support has expanded as ties with France and regional institutions deteriorated. Persistent jihadist violence continues to threaten mining corridors, transport links, and state control outside major cities.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal is strengthening Mauritania's energy position, but dependence on foreign operators, export infrastructure, and cross-border arrangements limits immediate sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Port Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore exports remain concentrated around SNIM and the Nouadhibou corridor. Expansion of ports, railways, and renewable-energy projects will require substantial foreign capital, creating exposure to external lenders and contractors.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Indian Ocean Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is strengthening its sovereignty claims and maritime position around the Chagos Archipelago while balancing relations with the United Kingdom, India, and other security partners.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital and Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: The country remains dependent on international finance, tourism, shipping, and undersea digital links. Competition among India, China, Gulf investors, and Western partners provides leverage but also creates strategic balancing pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Politics
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control of Western Sahara and its phosphate, fisheries, and renewable-energy assets remains contested by Algeria, the Polisario Front, and legal challenges affecting foreign partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Investment and Water Stress
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale renewable, hydrogen, port, and automotive projects are expanding Morocco's industrial sovereignty but rely on external technology and capital. Severe water stress could constrain energy, agriculture, and mining ambitions.

highlights: Cabo Delgado security remains the gatekeeper for LNG
Foreign capital dominates strategic gas development

frictionVectors.title: LNG Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency in Cabo Delgado continues to constrain the timing and operating environment of major gas projects. Mozambique relies heavily on foreign security assistance and multinational operators to protect extraction infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Corridor Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, roads, and gas logistics remain vulnerable to conflict and uneven state capacity, limiting domestic value capture from resource exports.

highlights: Oil discoveries raise bargaining power and local-content demands
Green hydrogen ambitions attract strategic foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries could transform public revenues, but production-sharing terms, local participation, and environmental safeguards remain central sovereignty questions.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: European, Chinese, and Gulf-linked investors are competing for uranium, lithium, rare earths, and green-hydrogen assets. Namibia is seeking greater domestic processing without deterring capital.

highlights: Junta consolidates control over uranium and hydrocarbons
Sanctions and insecurity constrain export sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Foreign Operator Disputes
frictionVectors.details: The military government is asserting greater control over uranium assets and renegotiating the role of foreign companies, particularly European interests. Operational uncertainty and security risks threaten investment and production continuity.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Export Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Niger's crude exports depend on cross-border pipeline infrastructure and political access through neighboring states. Regional tensions, sanctions, and militant threats reduce the government's ability to monetize its resources independently.

highlights: Oil theft and infrastructure decay still erode state control

frictionVectors.title: Upstream Production Leakage
frictionVectors.details: Oil theft, pipeline vandalism, and insecurity continue to reduce effective state control over production and public revenues. International operators retain major influence over technical capacity and capital-intensive projects.

frictionVectors.title: Refinery and Fuel-Supply Power
frictionVectors.details: Expanded domestic refining can reduce import dependence, but crude-supply access, pricing disputes, and private-sector concentration create new sovereignty and regulatory risks.

highlights: Regional security posture protects strategic influence
Mineral-export credibility remains under external scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Networks
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security role and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo remain a major source of diplomatic pressure. Sanctions risk and strained relations with Western partners could affect investment and aid.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Strategic infrastructure and development programs rely substantially on foreign aid, development finance, and private capital. This supports state capacity but limits complete autonomy over economic priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Licensing Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe continues to court foreign partners for exploration in its maritime zone, but limited discoveries and weak administrative capacity constrain bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Reliance
frictionVectors.details: Port, energy, and connectivity projects depend heavily on foreign finance and technical assistance, creating long-term exposure to outside commercial and strategic interests.

frictionVectors.title: Contract Renegotiation Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater national participation and fiscal returns from existing offshore oil and gas projects involving foreign operators, risking investor uncertainty and arbitration.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ports, transport corridors, and energy infrastructure remain reliant on foreign capital and contractors, including Gulf, European, Chinese, and Turkish interests.

highlights: Blue Economy Remains the Sovereignty Core

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Access
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles gains revenue from distant-water tuna fleets but must balance licensing income and processing investment against concerns over depleted stocks and limited domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cooperation with India, France, the United States, and other partners improves maritime surveillance while requiring careful management of sovereignty sensitivities around port access and security activity.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mineral Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mining projects remain dominated by external firms, while disputes over taxation, land rights, environmental impacts, and local employment challenge state authority.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-Resources Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, and mine infrastructure is increasingly tied to foreign-backed operators, raising concerns that logistics assets and mineral policy are being shaped by concession holders.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil and Fisheries Access
frictionVectors.details: Foreign partners are positioning for access to Somalia's offshore hydrocarbons and fisheries, while weak regulatory enforcement limits the government's ability to secure transparent and nationally beneficial terms.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Security Rivalries
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, Ethiopia, and other actors compete for influence over ports, maritime security, and regional access, intensifying tensions involving Mogadishu, Somaliland, and neighboring states.

highlights: Grid and freight bottlenecks constrain sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Mining capital and beneficiation tensions
frictionVectors.details: South Africa retains substantial regulatory control over platinum, manganese and chrome, but relies on foreign investment and technology. Disputes over local beneficiation and ownership continue to test relations with multinational miners.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and rail system degradation
frictionVectors.details: Power shortages and unreliable freight corridors weaken state control over strategic industrial infrastructure. Private operators and external financiers are increasingly important to restoring logistics capacity.

highlights: Peace process tied to resource access

frictionVectors.title: Oil-export dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nearly all export revenue depends on oil moving through Sudanese infrastructure, leaving Juba vulnerable to pipeline disruption and bargaining by external operators. Production-sharing arrangements and opaque revenue flows limit sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security and aid leverage
frictionVectors.details: Uganda, Sudan and other regional actors retain influence through security, trade and transport links. Humanitarian dependence and elite competition over oil revenues continue to weaken institutional autonomy.

highlights: Ports and gold attract rival patrons

frictionVectors.title: Gold networks and external financing
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling finance competing armed actors while foreign buyers and regional intermediaries shape access to export channels. This diverts resource rents away from accountable state institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan, maritime access and aid corridors are strategic assets contested amid the civil war. Gulf, Egyptian, Russian and other external interests increase the risk that infrastructure decisions serve wartime patrons rather than national reconstruction.

highlights: Critical minerals and gas invite competition

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail partnership dependence
frictionVectors.details: The government is using rail, port and corridor projects to strengthen its position as an East African trade hub. Reliance on Chinese, Gulf and other external finance creates exposure over concession terms and long-term control.

frictionVectors.title: LNG and mineral bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Natural gas and critical-mineral projects could increase fiscal and industrial autonomy, but negotiations over taxation, local processing and environmental impacts remain sensitive. External investors retain substantial technological and capital leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Port-centered external dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé strengthens Togo's regional logistics role but depends on foreign capital, shipping networks and neighboring-market demand. Concession structures and customs revenues remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence and instability in the Sahel threaten northern transport corridors and require deeper security cooperation with outside partners. Expanded foreign assistance may improve resilience while increasing dependence on external intelligence and equipment.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration and Aid Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: European partners retain substantial leverage through migration-control agreements, financial support, and trade access. Tunisia seeks autonomy but faces pressure to police departures and accept returned migrants.

frictionVectors.title: Imported Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported hydrocarbons and uneven investment in renewables leaves Tunisia vulnerable to external price shocks and supplier leverage.

highlights: Oil corridor advances under external finance

frictionVectors.title: EACOP and Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline is strategically important but concentrates financing, construction, and market risks among foreign partners. Environmental disputes and sanctions-related pressure continue to challenge sovereign control over the project.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure Influence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects expand Uganda's infrastructure base while increasing exposure to debt-service and contractor dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Copper Ownership and Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is leveraging global demand for copper and critical minerals to renegotiate investment terms, but foreign firms still dominate capital, technology, and processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito, Tanzanian, and southern transport corridors compete for Zambia's mineral exports. External infrastructure partners could improve options while also shaping long-term trade dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and Mineral Concession Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors remain prominent in lithium, platinum, and gold, while Zimbabwe struggles to secure domestic processing and transparent value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Financial Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions, restricted finance, and currency instability push Harare toward alternative partners, especially China, while limiting its bargaining power and access to diversified investment.
